speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The sector has transformed significantly in recent years, in terms of the types of transactions and the persons, institutions and technology conducting these transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We must ensure that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) keeps abreast of these developments and that we equip it with the necessary tools to facilitate the development of these new products and services, while managing the risks involved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: There are two key angles in this Bill that will improve MAS' effectiveness in doing this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For instance, the proper management of technology risk and measures to instill proper conduct amongst professionals in the financial sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Second, it addresses regulatory challenges presented by the digitalisation and transformation of financial markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: First, the need to enhance sector-wide regulatory effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS presently regulates the financial sector through various Acts, each of which focuses on specific sectors and activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, the Securities and Futures Act regulates the capital markets and its participants, while the Insurance Act deals with the activities of insurance firms and agents, amongst others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And because the regulatory framework is structured in this manner, certain MAS powers, such as the power to issue prohibition orders, or POs, or the power to impose technology risk management requirements, can be found in the different Acts, sometimes in differing forms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: They may also not be found in all of the MAS-administered Acts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For instance, the current powers to issue POs only apply to persons who provide capital markets services, financial advisory services or insurance services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And this is clearly not comprehensive enough, as it leaves out other traditional sectors, such as banking, as well as newer ones, like payment services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: There are also other powers in the MAS Act which cut across the different sectors within the financial sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, vastly more financial transactions are now conducted digitally through mobile applications and virtual assets, such as bitcoins and non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are becoming more common globally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS is committed to facilitating growth opportunities presented by digital finance and the cheaper and more convenient services it often brings for consumers, while guarding against new risks involved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These digital transformations could disrupt and challenge existing regulatory frameworks, which were designed for more traditional forms of financial transactions and services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, digital tokens service providers, or DT service providers, could easily structure their businesses to evade regulation in any one jurisdiction as they operate mainly online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill also enhances MAS' powers to ensure that FIs bolster their security and resilience of digital services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In short, to continue safeguarding Singapore's financial stability and maintaining public confidence in our financial sector, we must update our regulatory and enforcement framework to plug existing gaps and keep up with new risks emerging from an increasingly integrated, digitised and complex financial market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS has consulted both the industry and the public and received broad support for the FSM Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS has then incorporated the feedback received into the FSM Bill, where appropriate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The FSM Bill provides MAS with broad powers to impose POs against persons who have shown themselves to be unfit to perform key roles, activities and functions in the financial industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: POs are issued in cases of serious misconduct, such as to individuals who have been convicted of fraud or dishonesty in respect of their dealings with customers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The issuance of such POs can also deter others from committing similar lapses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, there are limitations to MAS' current PO powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS can only issue POs to certain specified persons under the Financial Advisors Act, or FAA, the Securities and Futures Act (SFA) and the Insurance Act (IA), such as trading representatives and insurance agents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, there are people who work in the financial industry who do not fall within these existing categories.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, it would not be possible to issue a PO to a bank manager, unless he is also a person to whom POs may be issued under any of the three previously mentioned Acts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Furthermore, while MAS has been decisive in issuing POs to individuals who have committed serious misconduct, such as in the 1MDB case, its powers have only enabled it to prohibit individuals from carrying out key regulated activities under the three Acts, such as providing financial advisory services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS' existing powers do not extend to prohibiting persons from carrying out other activities, including providing payment services or conducting other important functions in the financial industry, such as risk management or compliance and the administration of critical systems.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The FSM Bill broadens the categories of persons who may be subject to POs, rationalises the grounds for issuing POs, from a list of specific criteria to a single fit and proper test, and widens the scope of prohibition to cover functions that are critical to the integrity and functioning of financial institutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The revised PO powers are broadly aligned with those in Australia, Hong Kong, the UK and the US.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS will continue to exercise its PO powers judiciously, taking into account the nature and severity of each misconduct and its actual and potential impact on trust in our financial sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Existing checks and balances will continue to apply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Before MAS issues a PO to any person, the person has an opportunity to make representations to MAS and, if MAS proceeds with issuing a PO, the person has the right to appeal to the Minister.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) has strengthened international standards for virtual assets service providers, or VASPs, in June 2019, for this purpose.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We have already made amendments to existing legislation to implement these enhanced standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: VASPs are termed as digital token service providers for the purpose of the FSM Bill and I shall refer to them as DT service providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Entities that conduct the business of providing DT services in Singapore are subject to current legislation, regardless of where they are established.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, DT service providers created in Singapore, but without providing any DT services in Singapore, are currently unregulated for AML/CFT.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Further, these entities may claim to be headquartered here to take advantage of Singapore's global reputation, and this creates reputational risks for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Where a DT service provider established in one jurisdiction does not provide services in that jurisdiction, but offers its services digitally to other markets, the gap in the current global regulatory framework leads to no single jurisdiction having sufficient regulatory hold over the DT service provider for its ML/TF controls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To close this gap, the enhanced FATF standards require DT service providers to be at least licensed or registered in the jurisdiction, or jurisdictions, where they are created.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Persons that provide DT services in Singapore will continue to be regulated under existing MAS administered Acts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The FSM Bill will regulate such DT service providers a new class of FIs, primarily for ML/TF risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS will also impose other requirements on DT service providers, such that they have a meaningful presence in Singapore and MAS has adequate supervisory oversight over them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The AML/CFT requirements imposed on DT service providers will be aligned with the requirements imposed on digital payment token service providers regulated under the Payment Services Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill consolidates existing TRM requirements made under various MAS-administered Acts by introducing powers within the FSM Bill that apply to any FI or class of FIs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The powers will enable MAS to impose requirements in TRM, as well as in the safe and sound use of technology to deliver financial services and to protect data.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As I mentioned earlier, FIs today rely heavily on technology to deliver financial services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, the current maximum penalties that can be imposed for breaches of TRM requirements are not commensurate with the potential widespread impact to FIs' customers and the financial industry that could result from such breaches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: A technology event which impacts an FI's customers or other industry participants could involve breaches of several TRM requirements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: So, this means that an FI could face a much higher than $1 million financial penalty for a serious cyber attack or disruption to essential financial services where multiple breaches of TRM requirements are established, for example, an ATM network disruption or online trading disruption.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The quantum proposed is intended to underscore the critical importance of TRM to FIs' operations and the sound functioning of our financial system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The quantum was derived after considering existing penalty regimes of various other jurisdictions and Singapore Government agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, a contravention of the relevant provisions in the Telecommunications Act and Personal Data Protection Act can attract a financial penalty of $1 million.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In Hong Kong, a breach of data protection requirements can result in a financial penalty of HK$1 million.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In addition to the penalty imposed for a breach of TRM requirements, MAS is empowered to take other supervisory actions, such as requiring FIs to set aside additional regulatory capital until MAS is satisfied that adequate technology risk control measures have been put in place to address deficiencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Lastly, let me speak on the statutory protection from liability for mediators, adjudicators and employees of an operator of an approved dispute resolution scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Presently, an adjudicator, employee, officer or representative of the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre, or FIDREC, which operates an approved financial dispute resolution scheme, is contractually conferred certain protection from claims by a complainant or an FI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It will also position Singapore to strengthen our role and reputation as a safe, trusted and innovative global financial centre that creates good jobs and opportunities for our people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On this Bill, I would like to raise some clarifications and suggestions on managing the regulatory costs or burden on market participants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are grouped into three main areas – the need for a coherent and consistent regulatory framework, avoiding over-regulation and guarding against unintended burdens on entities or individuals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first area is the continuing push for a coherent and consistent regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our regulatory requirements should be easy to understand so that market participants do not have to waste time and costs trying to figure them out, or to "over-comply" on the safe side.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I, therefore, applaud the efforts to adopt a financial sector-wide regulatory approach in the consolidation of some of MAS' regulatory powers into this one Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My first question is whether this Bill is merely the first step in a broader exercise to rationalise our regulations on a financial sector-wide basis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will we gradually see the transposition of more pieces of our regulatory fabric into this FSM Bill, if passed?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This could allow us to surface and harmonise the possible inconsistencies in related regulations or how they are implemented.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is one part of this Bill that seems to cut against a financial sector-wide regulatory approach.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I understand it, digital token service providers who are providing such services in Singapore will continue to be licensed and regulated under the more extensive requirements in the Payment Services Act, the Securities and Futures Act and/or the Financial Advisers Act.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I support the implementation of the Financial Action Task Force's (FATF) recommendation to ensure that virtual asset service providers are at least regulated in their home jurisdiction for money laundering and terrorist financing (ML/TF) risks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, we should also consider other regulatory aims, such as consumer protection, prudential safety and anti-market manipulation, even for those "export" service providers who only provide their digital token services outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even if a particular digital token service is being provided abroad, Singaporeans and Singapore may still be exposed to that digital token and its risks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, we may wish to subject Singapore token advertisers who advertise outside of Singapore to the same restrictions that had recently been issued to Digital Payment Token service providers regulated under the Payment Services Act.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The high level of Internet accessibility and connectivity that Singaporeans enjoy means that we can no longer so clearly separate what is inside and outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Subjecting regulated digital token service providers to the same rules, regardless of whether they are providing digital token services inside or outside Singapore, would simplify compliance for them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would avoid the situation where a single digital token service provider is potentially subject to different legislation and regimes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, that probably turns on the following deeper questions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Has MAS studied crypto and virtual assets sufficiently to rationalise the piecemeal guidance it has issued to respond to specific issues and to articulate its holistic strategy to regulate such assets?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another question that I have is whether MAS has considered carving out such "export" service providers from licensing and regulation under the FSM Act if they are already being regulated in another jurisdiction which enforces the FATF Standards at the minimum, for example, where their services are being provided.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would prevent duplicative compliance costs from having to comply with the multiple regulatory regimes but still meet the FATF's intent to mitigate the risk of regulatory arbitrage.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Excessive compliance burdens can cause market participants to re-evaluate whether they should continue operating out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such "offshoring" not only reduces jobs and opportunities, but also hinders the development of an ecosystem in budding areas like fintech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Clause 29 of the Bill empowers MAS to impose requirements of TRM on any FI it regulates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we are recovering from the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, some have also opined that MAS should take a more supportive and facilitative approach by helping FIs scale up on TRM, instead of threatening FIs with a big stick.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Considering Singapore's aim to nurture a wider fintech ecosystem, including for startups, could MAS perhaps instead consider requiring any prospective licensees to present adequate cybersecurity plans as a condition for granting or renewing licences?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This was a suggestion which I had mooted in this House last year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such cybersecurity plans could include risk management measures, such as security audits of systems and servers and regular bug bounty programmes, to identify gaps ahead of malicious hackers, facilitating job and development opportunities for local white hat hackers and other cybersecurity talents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Like the Personal Data Protection Commission, MAS could stipulate the existence and extent of such voluntary plans and undertakings as an additional factor to mitigate any penalty that is imposed on a regulated entity if a breach or disruption event occurs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will replace the MAS' existing powers to issue POs to different individuals on different grounds under different legislation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a preliminary question, when will this new PO regime be brought into effect?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And MAS' consultation response suggests that sufficient notice will be given before the PO provisions are brought into effect, even after this Bill passes into law.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A key change is the broadened categories of persons who may be subject to POs, beyond employees of FIs performing regulated functions and including the service providers of FIs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the defence of taking all reasonable steps to ensure compliance and reasonable belief of compliance allow FIs to simply "shift" the regulatory burden to its service providers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would not seem fair to allow a bigger and better-resourced FI to rely on its service provider's contractual warranties and covenants, and effectively pass the regulatory burden to a smaller service provider who might not primarily operate in the regulated financial sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would make it easier for all FIs and/or their service providers to comply with the PO regime.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must also be conscious of the impact caused to individuals who have been, or may in the future be, issued with a PO.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the expanded scope for which POs may be issued, FIs may require some clarity in the form of MAS' guidance on the specific scope of POs issued in the newly-extended areas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Any ambiguity could create employee deployment issues for FIs and may drive them to terminate or refrain from hiring persons who have been issued with a PO entirely.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there any data or study on the number of persons who had previously been issued with a PO and who have, thereafter, returned to the financial sector?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As MAS has explicitly noted, POs materially affect individual livelihoods and we must calibrate the impact of POs precisely.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While it is important to prevent unfit persons from performing specific roles in the financial sector and to deter others from committing similar misconduct, we should ensure that those who have made mistakes are punished adequately for their errors, and no more.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In that vein, can I ask the Minister if an individual's previous PO can be purged from the records after a specific period of time?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must constantly revisit this balance to stay ahead of rapid technological and other developments and to keep our lead as a market-leading and trusted financial centre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Those of us who have travelled or lived in the US may be aware that if we open a bank or credit card statement and we notice an unrecognised transaction, we would simply call the financial institution, report the incident and, in most instances, the customer service officer will, eventually, remove the error transaction, often after some investigation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I used to view this as an anomalous luxury, the sort of sociocultural exceptionalism that only a global financial superpower like the US will be able to conjure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I now understand that, much like the ability to return goods, no questions asked, within a stipulated timeframe or the ability to access long-term fixed-term mortgages, these features of economic life result from regulatory and legislative choices that the US has chosen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, many other OECD economies have weaved together laws and regulations that afford much more financial protection for the average consumer than we have been able to muster.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such consolidation is welcomed, of course, not least because it renders transparent the full scope of rules and regulations MAS oversees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The omnibus Bill is wide-ranging and touches on matters as diverse as anti-money laundering (AML) and combating financing of terrorism (CFT) provisions, requirements for technology risk management and statutory protection for financial dispute resolution agents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I support the Bill, I will focus my remarks on Part 5, which have to do with technology risk management.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will do so through the lens of the consumer and, in particular, consumer protection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Before I proceed, I declare that I am the Chief Economist Emeritus of a wealth management advisory outfit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The number of scam cases has steadily risen and this trend is unlikely to retreat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am certain that many of us have had residents come to us for help with banking scams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For the recent OCBC phishing scam alone, I had two different residents wo reached out to me.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The scams had wiped out their life savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And I felt helpless – not as helpless as they did – but I certainly felt helpless that I could not offer more than to reach out to the banking institutions to share their side of the story, reassure them that the Police were working on resolving their cases and offer to follow up with agencies that they felt were not being responsive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I could not tell them that Parliament was working to better protect them and others like them with the specific force of law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As online services become increasingly the norm in Singapore, the opportunities and incentives for bad actors will increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While banking scams are impossible to completely eradiate, we can better manage the acceptable level of risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But our legislative efforts have largely been cautionary, by encouraging individuals to exercise the appropriate cyber-hygiene, as if we needed another type of hygiene situation to worry about; or reactive, when the Police force is mostly left with belated attempts to track down and apprehend perpetrators, many of whom will never ever be found, or will fall beyond the reach of our current laws.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The banking sector, to date, has appealed to the viability of self-regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, on paper, some of these additional protections may have helped prevent some instances of fraud, had they been operative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As I shared then, we were able to do so without any two-factor authentication (2FA), beyond the PIN.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We have since repeated the experiment – all good science must be replicable – and I can confirm that we were still able to breach the stated limits without a token.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, even the most finely-tuned stipulations will be of limited efficacy if the tokens themselves are not deployed as intended.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, lapses of this nature are not isolated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another customer shared about how her mother's credit card limit was breached by almost two times, without any alert or the credit line being frozen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have had residents share with me about how, after they had inadvertently released their banking information to the scammer, they realised their mistake and, within the following hour, called the bank to request forfeiting of further transactions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the long hold times and, ironically, security verification procedures meant that the fraudulent transfers could take place in the interim.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As experts in the financial world, banks and their staff hold a duty of care to their customers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They hold a far greater knowledge of the inner workings of illegal modus operandi – money mules, laundering, impersonation, scam rings – than the average customer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, they have access to the customer's banking history, which can be used to detect anomalies or deviations in their regular behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Scams and phishing operations have grown so sophisticated that the average layperson – not to mention those who are not comfortable with technology – cannot always be reasonably expected to routinely identify and proactively avoid them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, such due diligence is already exercised in limited form today, which means that it is clearly doable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Software-led detection of anomalous transactions has been employed by American credit card companies for decades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More recent advances in big data and machine learning have refined such techniques even further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This still leaves enormous leeway for how banks currently choose to handle scam cases, with very limited recourse for the consumer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a nation, we have never shied away from complementing regulation with legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is little reason for us to revise this now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In principle, the Government has already tools to enforce greater discipline on banks to ensure that consumers are better protected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But there are reasons why the banking regulator, MAS, has been a little more reactive than proactive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, banking regulation is but one of many, many hats that MAS wears.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MAS is, simultaneously, the lender of last resort, banker to the Government, guardian of inflation, executor of exchange rate policy, promoter of financial development, overseer of financial stability and financial sector regulator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Setting aside how such a multiplicity of objectives may occasionally come into conflict, the many objectives make it difficult for a single regulator to monitor and ensure coherence between them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, in its efforts to foster greater financial sector development, MAS may be more comfortable with allowing banks to experiment with innovations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is not an issue, on its face, but the risk is that the costs of such innovations end up being disproportionately borne by the end user.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Admittedly, supporting banking innovation and entrepreneurship requires some degree of regulatory forbearance, but, by the same token, this may, in turn, foster an aversion towards excessive or overzealous enforcement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Third, the proof of the pudding truly is in the eating.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MAS has not always appeared to be aware of the blind spots, or, if it has, it has been reticent to act quickly and decisively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if we wish for MAS to retain overall oversight responsibility over the financial sector, as implied by the consolidations weaved into this Bill, it is still reasonable to have an independent consumer financial protection arm, operating within the broader ambit of MAS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The financial protection arm would receive complaints from the public on consumer finance, such as deposits, mortgages, credit cards, an auto and education loans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It would also examine compliance with regulations, from the standpoint of end-user.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this manner, we will have distinct departments addressing concerns raised by the consumer and producer which, in this case, is the banking sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A Chinese wall could then shield this body from the various prudential supervision departments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the past, there was a market and business conduct department, which ostensibly served the, and I quote, "interests of depositors, investors and policyholders".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This may have since been enfolded into the corporate finance and consumer department.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In either case, however, these appear to work more with market professionals and possibly sophisticated investors, rather than the retail consumer, nor does the department appear to be empowered to advocate on behalf of the consumer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we can go beyond regulation, even the beefed-up kind I have suggested, to introduce outright consumer financial protection legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This can be independent of existing regulatory and consumer education efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some see regulation and legislation as essentially two sides of the same coin.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At risk of seeming pedantic, this is a distinction with a difference.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Regulation is a function of Government agencies and the domain of bureaucrats, while legislation is debated, deliberated and realised in this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Regulation has one clear advantage over legislation: because it falls under the purview of a governmental agency – in this case, MAS – it does not have to undergo the Bills process, it can be more nimble than full-bore legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By the same token, however, codifying essential principles into legislation enshrines the doctrines that we wish to remain inerrant and allows them to remain invariant to the vagaries of specific implementation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Just as important, laws embed the democratic process in the way that regulatory machinations never quite can.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many other jurisdictions have specific consumer protection laws.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the US, the Fair Credit Billing Act was enacted as far back as 1974 and requires prompt written acknowledgement of billing disputes and the investigation of billing errors by creditors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In 2010, the Consumer Financial Protection Act was passed, establishing an independent agency within the Federal Reserve to regulate the offering and provision of consumer financial products.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The United Kingdom Consumer Credit Act provides a number of comparable protections and, in the European Union, the Revised Directive on Payment Services encapsulates a number of regulations governing financial service providers, including requiring strong customer authentication for the majority of electronic payments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Implementing legislation for stronger consumer protection does not absolve individuals of their responsibility to practise good cyber-hygiene.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, at the very least, it will shift the burden of defending against such unscrupulous behaviour away from resting almost entirely on the shoulders of the household and bring businesses, in particular, banks, into the risk-sharing picture as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And just as we do not rely solely on mediation mechanisms, such as TADM and TAFEP, to fully govern our labour disputes, we can further support consumer rights in finance with appropriate legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Financial institutions would also be more inclined to pursue unauthorised purchases with the merchant and, these merchants, in turn, would be more careful in accepting potentially fraudulent payments, else they lose their right to accept that mode of payment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rudimentary small-claims insurance schemes would also emerge, with costs often absorbed by the financial institutions themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will this increase the cost of doing business?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the point is that the cost of policing e-commerce fraud and theft was always there; it was simply absorbed almost entirely by the consumer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such a law would spread the risk among all actors in the economy: the buyer, the seller and the financial intermediary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is an idea whose time has come.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: With digitalisation speeding up the pace of Financial Sector transformation, it is important for MAS to continue to refresh our regulations to preserve trust and confidence in Singapore’s financial industry.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given the above, I believe that the new provisions contained in the Financial Services and Markets Bill are timely and sound.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is on this basis that I would like to seek some clarifications on how this Bill will be implemented for the clarity of the public and those in the industry.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On the Harmonised and Expanded Power of MAS to Issue Prohibition Orders (POs) to bar persons in the financial industry.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One, presumably, POs will, generally, be issued only if a person has a former, existing or prospective nexus to the financial industry.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As the provision of financial services is complex, with many ecosystems, partners, how will proximity be assessed to define nexus?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will staff from a financial institutions' (FIs) service providers such as IT vendors, and ecosystem partners, such as e-commerce platforms, be subjected to a PO?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Two, while the basis for streamlining the disparate grounds for issuing POs under the Security and Futures Act (SFA), Financial Advisors Act (FAA) and Insurance Act (IA) into a single fit-and-proper test under section 188 of the Bill is sound, the effectiveness of such a test hinges on how it will be applied.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, can the Minister clarify if there will be a retrospective application of such assessments for persons with past misconduct that might not have been caught under the three statutes, but who may be deemed as not fit and proper under the new test?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If so, will prohibitions commence from the point of misconduct?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, Singapore has a considerable number of foreign talents partnering our local workforce to deliver cutting-edge financial products and services.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given this, can the Minister clarify if existing and incoming foreign talent will also be subjected to the same due diligence as that for local staff?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If so, will there be clearer guidelines on how background checks will be conducted?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The reason for this question is that since the misconduct in critical functions could be non-regulated activities, it, therefore, may not be captured in overseas registries.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This could impact the effectiveness of the fit-and-proper test for foreign talents.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Three, this Bill has broadened the scope of MAS to issue POs covering activities beyond MAS-administered Acts.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This would now include serious misconduct in activities, such as funds management, risk and technology management per section 7(2) of the Bill, which were previously not covered, and for all roles beyond senior management or material risk takers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This puts the Bill and, therefore, all on notice that everyone has a role to play in managing risks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the severity thresholds of a misconduct and how proportionality of misconduct and the prohibitions will apply, since this can be subjective, given different activities?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As the risk of any activity is a collective effort of everyone in the value chain from junior staff to senior management, how will MAS assess culpability of a misconduct across the ranks?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I am encouraged that this Bill has instituted safeguards to balance MAS' increased powers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As a person’s appeal must be referred by the Minister to an Advisory Committee selected from a Panel, can the Minister clarify the considerations for independence of the Committee and/or Panel?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I ask this as those in the financial industry often share close networks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: And section 14 of the Bill provides for panel members to be eligible for re-appointment.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Also, in addition to the right of appeal to the Minister, may a person who has been issued with a PO bring his or her appeal case to Court?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given the intense competition from fintechs, FIs have themselves been transforming and digitalising their businesses by a combination of outsourcing as well as adopting cutting-edge technologies, such as Software as a Service.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In cases where third party cloud-based solutions, such as Amazon Web Services or Google Cloud, are being adopted, it is known as an industry norm that FIs have no ability to conduct independent audits on such providers despite these services being critical.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given these limitations, how will MAS weigh the accountability on FIs should negligence fall on the part of such providers?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I agree that this is important to align our regulations with the standards set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to guard against money laundering and terrorism financing risks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: MAS had in response to a recent Parliamentary Question stated that non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are currently not regulated by MAS, given that the underlying assets are predominantly art and other collectibles, with MAS taking a technology-neutral stance as it “looks through” to the underlying characteristics.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, will MAS consider having oversight of NFTs in this Bill or other existing legislation soon?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my speech today, I would like to touch on the topic of virtual assets and how this rapidly evolving area of finance is increasingly gaining prominence and relevance globally and, therefore, how Singapore can continue to evolve our approach to stay ahead as a key financial centre of the world.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Two years ago, in late 2020, I spoke about the Payment Services (Amendment) Bill, where I noted then that bitcoin was at a record high of around US$34,000, having risen almost fourfold over the course of 2020, far surpassing the previous high of around $19,800 set around December 2017, just before its precipitous crash in the months after.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many have called bitcoin and cryptocurrencies a massive bubble then and some still do now.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Fast forward to today, bitcoin is now at or around US$46,000 but not without reaching an all-time high of almost $69,000 and a low of $29,000 just within the last 52 weeks alone.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just as how cryptocurrencies are not solely about bitcoin and its rise and fall, virtual assets are not just about cryptocurrencies, and blockchain technology does not just apply to virtual assets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The term "virtual" conveys the sense that it is somehow not as real as, say, physical assets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But today, one's digital identity and persona are perhaps even more significant than those in the physical world.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just ask any influencer who spends most of his or her time in the digital world, be it Facebook, Instagram or even TikTok.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Virtual assets are not solely about individuals buying an NFT to display on their personal social media profiles, however.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The chairman of BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, noted in his recent letter to shareholders that "BlackRock is studying digital currencies, stablecoins and the underlying technologies to understand how they can help us serve our clients".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was also the same person who called bitcoin "an index of money laundering." At the same time, the Ukraine-Russia conflict also saw the Ukraine government conducting fundraising via cryptocurrencies and NFTs and with Russia also supposedly considering accepting bitcoin as payment for its oil and gas exports.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The bottom line is that in the modern world, purely virtual creations can, indeed, have value, so long as enough people accept that to be the case.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: By and large, I do agree that MAS has been proactive in studying the development of this industry very early on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Project Ubin, for example, was announced all the way back in November 2016 to explore the use of blockchain and distributed ledger technology.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The final phase of the project concluded in July 2020, but, as pointed out by my colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim during the Committee of Supply debates earlier this year, after expending significant effort and resources to better understand the nature, function and practical operation surrounding the possibility of a digital currency issued by our central bank, the conclusion is that there is no pressing need for its issuance at this time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was despite several advantages to moving early on the issuance, such as crowding out alternatives, such as unbacked and inherently volatile digital private currencies, through stable, well-designed Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs), allow for the application of more innovative monetary policy, especially with regard to disinflation, and help reduce the incidence of counterfeiting and illicit activities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As noted in the White House factsheet on US President Biden's Executive Order on ensuring responsible development of digital assets, over 100 countries today are exploring or piloting CBDCs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And, in China, after launching the digital Yuan domestically, such digital Yuan payment services were also introduced to visitors of the recent Beijing Winter Olympics.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given the early stages of most central banks' work into CBDCs, this should be one area in which Singapore can demonstrate global leadership in.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A related point is one which I have raised back in 2020 about the progress made in assessing payment service provider applications and the slow pace at which approvals were given.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Subsequently, in response to my Parliamentary Question in July 2021, it was noted that since the commencement of the Payment Services Act, MAS had received over 480 licence applications.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, back then, MAS had not issued any licence to Digital Payment Tokens (DPT) service providers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I note several in-principle approvals since then, such as that for DBS, Independent Reserve, FOMO Pay, Coinhako, TripleA, Paxos, BTC and Hodlnaut.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At last count though, I still see 163 companies that are currently on the exemption list.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, announced in December last year that it has withdrawn its licence application to operate here in Singapore and has since shut down its operations here in February.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While it is debatable whether it is a loss for Singapore per se, to be clear, I am not calling for licences to be hastily awarded, but we also need to recognise that there are firms still allowed to operate under a transitional exemption, regardless of their merits, until their applications are approved or rejected.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, getting their applications approved or rejected expeditiously not only gets rid of potential bad actors, but allows responsible market players to move forward with their business plans, entrench their operations here in Singapore for the long term and contribute to the vibrancy and innovation in the sector here.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the MAS 2020 Licencing and Registration Report for Capital Markets Intermediaries, I note that MAS is committed to a four-month timeframe for processing corporate licence and registration applications with the mean and median time taken not too far off from the four-month service standard.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, I hope more resources can be devoted to ensuring that we help to support and facilitate the responsible development of the virtual asset industry in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Next, I would like to touch on the ban on marketing and advertising by service providers of DPTs as announced by MAS in January this year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I wonder whether an outright ban unique to DPTs is an appropriate means of protecting consumers and consistent with the approach in which MAS regulates the advertising of other investment products and services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge and agree with MAS' view that the trading of cryptocurrencies is highly risky and not suitable for the general public per se.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, single stock investing is also highly risky in my view.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Grab and SEA, for example, among Singapore’s largest companies by market cap, saw their share prices decline 40% to 50% in the year-to-date alone, with SEA down 60% to 70% from its 52-week high.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What I am most concerned with, however, are complex derivative products available to retail investors that even I myself struggle to understand, such as Contracts for Difference (CFDs), which, in itself, is an instrument which is banned for sale to retail investors in the United States and Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recall hearing ads for CFDs on the radio just a few months ago and even reading branded content on The Straits Times about how these products can supposedly allow investors to manage trading risks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ironic in my view, given that it can be a product with 10 times leverage, with risks of a complete wipe-out of the investment within a short period of time and which is significantly riskier than an equivalent unleveraged financial instrument.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do not think that having a standard boiler plate, “this advertisement has not been reviewed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore” and long paragraphs of text in fine print are sufficient measures for financial institutions to absolve themselves of their responsibilities towards retail investors.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But perhaps advertising by DPT service providers could also come within the scope of the fair and balanced advertising and other advertising restrictions, as covered under the securities and futures regulations and financial advisers’ regulations, with the rules holistically reviewed and finetuned collectively to ensure that all financial market participants do not merely present a one-sided view of potential investment products in their advertisements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, more should be done in terms of continuing financial education and improving the financial literacy of the population at large and to help everyone understand the underlying risks and rewards of their investments, be it in Ethereum or equities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, no discussion on cryptocurrencies is complete without an appreciation of the money laundering and terrorist financing risks it presents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To this end, I note that the Bill will align the scope of digital token services to the enhanced Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would MAS end up being inundated with transactional data, given the low threshold, and how would MAS manage the risks of having questionable transactions slip through the cracks versus being overwhelmed with data which could end up expending resources to investigate too many suspicious transactions which were flagged out, which could otherwise turn out to be legitimate?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the Singapore FinTech Festival in November last year, MAS Managing Director Ravi Menon spoke about crypto-based activities, noting that “not to get into this game, I think risks Singapore being left behind.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, fundamental to the development of sound financial markets is the maintenance of integrity of institutions and the personnel supporting these institutions in the face of technological disruptions and extensive cross-border capital flows.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The question is: why does it matter that we have a fit-for-purpose regulatory framework that supports integrity of personnel and financial institutions and is resilient to technological disruptions and increased cross-border activities?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: I suggest that there are two reasons that it matters.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: First, a regulatory framework that supports the integrity of personnel and financial institutions leads to trust.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The facilitation of financial intermediation that will benefit both customers and investors in the modern economy requires a system of secure property rights that remains appropriate under different circumstances.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the current era, digital transformation has the potential to disrupt the way businesses are conducted even while it provides new opportunities for customers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: While there exist incentives for private enforcement when parties that are engaged in financial transactions have repeated interactions over time, the new digital world of more anonymous transactions may require public enforcement, such as through financial sector-wide regulation encapsulated in the FSM Bill, to protect the rights of parties to a financial contract.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In order to attract funds to risky ventures, individuals or firms undertaking them have to promise their investors a risk premium.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The FSM Bill, in seeking to develop an appropriate financial system to suit current circumstances, enables financiers operating from Singapore to reduce the risk premium required of a borrower by spreading the risk across a larger number of investors.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The problems of adverse selection and moral hazard inherent in financing can be mitigated by the wider availability of information that investors have about borrowers, leading to the wider availability of credit at lower risk premiums.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve this, it is necessary that managers and personnel working in the financial industry be trustworthy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Second, with extensive cross-border capital flows, maintaining a good international reputation delivers important benefits.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Having foreign capital and financial institutions in Singapore can help to lower the cost of capital.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: By promoting competition with the domestic financial sector, it can also improve the allocation of capital to productive uses.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, firms that serve overseas customers and investors reap the benefits of economies of scale.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Establishing a good reputation shapes the expectations of market participants and increases their confidence in making financial transactions across international borders.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: With the end of what is called the first Age of Globalisation that coincided with World War I, there followed a period of disruption to international capital flows and global trade in goods and services.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, there soon emerged a second Age of Globalisation that started roughly in 1960 and has continued to the present.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: While the emerging geopolitical tensions may, ultimately, lead to a new international economic order, it seems fair to say that our existing law and institutions should still be structured to harness the advantages that financial globalisation can deliver.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The provision in the FSM Bill to regulate all virtual asset service providers created in Singapore that provide virtual asset services outside of Singapore helps us to maintain a strong international reputation as a financial centre.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: For people to be willing to participate in a financial market, they must perceive it to be safe and secure.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Regulators of the financial system must, therefore, make and enforce the rules to protect both customers and investors.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The FSM Bill seeks to ensure this through maintaining the integrity of institutions and the personnel supporting these institutions in the face of technological disruptions and extensive cross-border capital flows.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MAS’ future strategies will be informed by the close supervisory interactions with stakeholders in a rapidly evolving sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The measures proposed in the Bill should be implemented quickly so that potential investors in our market will not be in a position of jurisdictional arbitrage which may be disadvantageous to the Singapore market.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Investors and talent will be drawn to countries seen to be more accepting and supportive of this asset category, such as Estonia, Germany or the United Kingdom.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Presently, entities in the business of VAs here are subject to the Payment Services Act where the VAs are considered digital payment tokens.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: VAs are subject to the Securities and Futures Act or the Financial Advisers Act where the products are capital market products.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Moving forward, would the Ministry or MAS consider setting up a new category of market licence for VASPs and digital currency exchanges?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their regulatory standards should be comparable to those for licensed securities brokers and automated trading venues.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is in order to build a simple, secure and accessible digital assets ecosystem that will support VA investment in Singapore, while mitigating potential risks.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I propose a risk-based approach for the regulatory framework to identify digital asset services that pose sufficient risk to warrant regulation and where such risks are crucial to address.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Issues, such as the safe custody of assets, know-your-client (KYC) requirements, AML/CFT, market manipulation, accounting and auditing, risk management, conflicts of interest and the acceptance of virtual assets for trading, must be addressed.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MAS should require VA trading platforms to adopt an operational structure and use technology to offer client protection which is equivalent to traditional financial institutions in the securities sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, the market licence specifically for those service providers should not impose onerous obligations that might cause these businesses to be forced out by larger international operators which have services provided both physically and virtually.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to be mindful of ensuring a level playing field for VASPs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, any application of the existing financial services regulatory regime to digital asset businesses that would require compulsory professional indemnity insurance should take into account the current lack of availability of such insurance for digital asset service providers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is, implementation of a regulatory regime where compliance is not possible, has the same effect as an outright ban on these activities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As virtual asset trading platforms interface directly with the Singaporean public, MAS should, therefore, accept licensing applications from platform operators who are committed to and capable of complying with the expected licensing criteria and continuing conduct requirements.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, the licensee must obtain MAS' prior written approval for any plan or proposal to introduce or offer a new or incidental product, service or activity, or to make a material change to an existing service or activity.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MAS should require a platform operator to establish and implement written internal policies and governance procedures to ensure compliance with requirements concerning the custody of virtual assets.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A platform operator should also have adequate processes in place for handling requests for deposits and withdrawals of clients' virtual assets to guard against loss arising from theft, fraud and other dishonest acts, professional misconduct or omissions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singaporean consumers require confidence that they are able to access the products and services they desire at home, via legally regulated and compliant professionals, rather than by seeking out risky services in unregulated locations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The development of VAs will provide many new opportunities, including those in Singapore's technological sector, which can translate into more high-skilled jobs and growth-oriented investments, if the right balance is struck by the Government in approaching regulation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are opportunities for the larger accounting or audit firms, too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Established insurers and their brokers also need to be more open to providing insurance coverage and services for the virtual asset industry.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, a number of traditional financial institutions are seeking to develop their own cryptocurrencies on private blockchains to enable the instantaneous and cross-border transfer of payments.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Lastly, our Singapore Police Force must be well-situated to understand law enforcement priorities and strategic objectives in this area.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Its collaborative relationship with MAS is a key strength.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) reaffirmed in 2019 Singapore's financial sector oversight to be "among the best globally" and noted that MAS has struck a good balance in fostering financial innovation while strengthening regulatory oversight.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The exciting development since 2015 has been in the space of fintech.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has a vibrant fintech ecosystem with over 1,100 fintech firms serving consumers, businesses, and financial institutions across the different asset classes.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I congratulate MAS and our financial services institutions for enabling Singapore to "punch above our weight".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, imperative for Singapore, as a leading financial services centre, to be plugged in, into the latest developments, including digital currencies, crypto, digital tokens, NFTs, metaverse and the like.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These technologies disrupt but also offer immense opportunities for the industry and the markets at large.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With the proliferation of these technologies, there are risks of money laundering, terrorism funding, corruption and fraud, black market money supply and scams.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In view of the changing landscape in the financial services and market space, it is important that the Singapore financial sector oversight consider the proliferation of fintech and non-traditional financial institutions and service providers and include their activities under MAS' regulatory ambit.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The industry, including the Singapore FinTech Association, welcomes the FSM Bill.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They participated in the consultation and are supportive of this Bill and welcome the increase in transparency and accountability of all players, whose activities fall under the prescribed MAS' activities regulated or to be regulated.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They would like to request that MAS publish the clarifications from the consultation as frequently asked questions, or FAQs, on the website so that they can all refer to it.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to the proposal to regulate digital token service providers created in Singapore but carrying on a business of providing any type of digital token service outside Singapore, we understand that these digital payment token service providers must be licensed or registered in the jurisdiction where they are created and that "without imposing this requirement globally, regulatory arbitrage could occur where no single jurisdiction has sufficient regulatory hold over a specific digital payment token service provider".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We do seek clarification as to how a digital token service provider that falls within this category but is, in fact, already licensed and regulated in its overseas jurisdiction of operations, will be regulated by MAS.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is a concern that such double-regulation by two regulators may result in excessive compliance obligations and costs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, we note that the activity of providing advisory services relating to the offer or sale of digital tokens will be covered by the new legislation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The definition of "digital tokens" covers, one, both digital payment tokens, for example, bitcoin and ether; and, two, digital representations of a capital market product, that is, tokenised shares and bonds.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Following from this, digital token service providers created in Singapore but carrying on a business of providing advisory services relating to the offer or sale of digital payment tokens outside Singapore, will need to be licensed in Singapore, pursuant to the FSM Bill.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: However, would digital token service providers created in Singapore and undertaking the same business in Singapore need to be licensed in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this question as the provision of advisory services relating to digital payment tokens is not currently regulated under the Payment Services Act 2019 or under the Financial Advisers Act 2001.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These Acts would apply to businesses carrying on the business of providing regulated services in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Technology will continue to transform the financial services sector, affecting how organisations operate and how consumers conduct banking and financial activities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: New advancements in the banking and fintech industries will also impact the type of skills, talents and job roles needed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Skills across the board will need to be upgraded, both on the operations side as well as the governance and compliance side.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What are MAS' plans to enhance the skills and competencies of the financial services industry as well as the skills required in the ecosystem, from auditing to risk compliance to legal and insurance?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With the FSM Bill, MAS will have oversight of entities that deal with any potential alternative to the fiat currencies and "money supply".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is a welcome move as we have witnessed the speculative nature of bitcoins and cryptocurrencies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will MAS ensure that the general public in Singapore do not fall prey to scams involving bitcoins and the like?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Bitcoins and cryptocurrencies are built on blockchain technology.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Initiatives like DBS' Digital Exchange (DDEX) and SGX's Climate ImpactX are all to be applauded.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There will be new skills and new capabilities built in the industry even as we continue to exercise prudence in technology risk management.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, technology has led to a rapid increase and innovation in new financial products and assets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Conversely, the risks and challenges of managing these products and assets as well as the financial institutions and persons involved have also heightened.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support the consolidation and enhancement of the regulatory powers under this Bill to address the challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe that this will lead to a more holistic and comprehensive management of the financial services sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, can the Minister provide further clarification on the Harmonised and Expanded Powers to Issue Prohibition Orders (PO)?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If a person has been placed on a watchlist or issued something of equivalence to our PO by an overseas jurisdiction, would they be issued a PO here by default?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will facilitate various national regulators to better work together to maintain the integrity of global markets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill also states that persons who have been issued a PO may be, amongst other things, prohibited from becoming a substantial shareholder of a financial institution.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will it be an offence to wilfully assist the PO individual to evade the PO?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even with the PO, it is not difficult for seasoned fraudsters to set up their theatre here, with actors and props in tow.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Take, for example, the recent case of a blockchain company that is being investigated for cheating offences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One of the key personnel was previously convicted for commercial crimes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Usually, these cases only come to light after some of our citizens are cheated by these individuals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such incidents would make a mockery of our regulators in the way we oversee such theatrics.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: More than just putting up regulations and by-laws, we should look at the gaps in how we allow businesses to get registered.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
